title: They Are Deleting Words
deck: Newspeak does not merely forbid dissent. It deletes the distinctions a person needs to make an independent judgment.
body: Edition note: Complete English translation of the Chinese essay. Full-book spoilers.
Syme is a colleague of Winston's. He works on a dictionary at the Ministry of Truth.
One day over lunch, he begins talking about his work with great enthusiasm.

The eleventh edition of the Newspeak dictionary is nearly ready, he says. This will be the definitive edition; there will be no more revisions. What they are doing is cutting away the surplus parts of language.
You think our job is to make new words? he says. No. Our job is to destroy words.

He gives an example. Once you have “good,” “bad” is redundant: “ungood” will do. For greater intensity, there are “plusgood” and “doubleplusgood.” So a whole batch of words, “excellent,” “splendid,” “outstanding,” can all be deleted.
In the end, he says, the whole dictionary will be much thinner.
Then he says something Winston remembers for a long time.
By 2050, he says, not a single person will be able to understand the conversation we are having now.
What do they want?
Newspeak is usually treated as a satirical invention, a joke about the way official language dresses up an ugly reality.
It is not. It is the most serious technical proposal in the book.
The book explains this very directly. Newspeak is not intended to make speaking easier, or simply to make everyone repeat the same line.
Its purpose is to make certain thoughts physically impossible to think.

The logic runs like this: a person needs words to think. If “free” survives only in expressions such as “this dog is free from lice,” while its political meaning has been stripped away entirely, then a person has no way to think “I want to be free.” It is not that they dare not think it. They no longer have the parts with which to assemble the thought.
What Newspeak seeks, then, is not to forbid thoughtcrime. It is to make thoughtcrime something that cannot be said, and therefore cannot be thought.
This goes further than any form of censorship. Censorship stops something that has already come into being. Newspeak keeps it from coming into being at all.
Three components
Newspeak is not the whole of it. This is an entire design, every part aimed at the same goal.
First: Newspeak deals with language. It makes certain thoughts impossible to assemble.
Second: doublethink deals with contradiction.
This is one of the hardest concepts in the book to explain, and one of the most important. It means believing two contradictory things at the same time, without feeling a conflict.
Knowing that the past has been altered, for instance, while sincerely believing it has never been altered. Fabricating evidence while remaining certain that you are upholding the truth.
The key is the last part: without feeling a conflict.
Because if a person feels the conflict, that discomfort is an opening. They will think, ask questions, follow the matter further. That discomfort is precisely what doublethink is meant to eliminate.
Winston describes the operation in the book: knowing, then forgetting that you know; and once you have forgotten, forgetting the act of forgetting as well.
Third: rewriting the past deals with facts.

Winston's job is to alter old newspapers. Someone has been executed, so the record of the praise he once received must be removed. A prediction was wrong, so it must be changed to match what actually happened. Once the alteration is complete, the old copy goes into the “memory hole” to be burned.
Afterward, no original remains against which anything can be checked.
One sentence in the book puts this very precisely. Its sense is that if all the records tell the same story, the lie enters history and becomes fact.
These three operations together amount to one thing: deleting from existence whatever is not supposed to be there.
Not suppression. Not prohibition. Not intimidation. Deletion.
They do it very well
We need to be clear here about how effective this machinery is. Otherwise what follows will not stand.
It works.

Look at Winston's position. He knows the Party is lying: this is his trade; he alters the newspapers himself. He has a hazy memory of the old world. He secretly buys a notebook and begins keeping a diary.
And he cannot even clearly say what he is opposing.
On his first day with the diary, he cannot find anything to write. He knows he has something to say, but not what it is, or whom to say it to.
Later he remembers something: he once had a photograph, a photograph that could prove the Party was lying. He dropped it into the memory hole.
He understood what the photograph meant and hid it. About ten minutes later, he still burned it out of fear.
That is the machinery's power: it makes someone who knows what the evidence means destroy that evidence for it with his own hands, out of fear.
Consider Syme, too. He carries out this engineering of language. He understands the principles of Newspeak. He knows what he is deleting.
And it is because he understands too clearly that he is vaporized.
One day he does not come to work. His name disappears from a list. Winston thinks to himself: Syme no longer exists. He has never existed.
Notice those words: “has never.” This is not a figure of speech. Within this system, vaporizing a person means deleting every trace of him. He is not dead. He has never been.
But they want more than this
Now we come to the real center of this essay, the fuse that runs through all four essays on the novel.
The three operations above all deal with things outside the person: language, records, public accounts.
But the system's goal goes further.
The book makes this very clear. O'Brien will explain it more explicitly later, but it is already visible in the first half: the Party is not satisfied with people's obedience.
Obedience is not enough.
Someone who obeys still holds a thought inside: “I am being forced.” Outwardly he complies; inwardly he knows he is complying. That knowing is something that has not been deleted.

Winston writes a sentence in his diary, one of the best-known sentences in the first half of the book: freedom means being free to say that two plus two equals four. Once that is granted, everything else follows.
As he writes it, he feels he has grasped something unshakable.

Because two plus two equals four needs no one's permission. It does not depend on the Party, on records, or on anyone's recognition. You can strip a person of everything, and this will still be what it is in his mind.
It is the last thing he has.
And the third essay will return to this: it is precisely the last thing they intend to take away.
That “definitive edition”
Let us return to what Syme said.
The eleventh edition of Newspeak will be the definitive edition.
This is a strange thing to say. How can a dictionary have a definitive edition? Language is alive. New words grow; new uses arise.
Unless your aim is not to record a language, but to finish constructing something closed.
And “closed” is the key to understanding this whole design.

Look at what these operations have in common: Newspeak deletes words until no surplus remains; doublethink removes the feeling of contradiction; rewriting the records ensures that no original remains for comparison.
Each operation closes a gap.

The gaps in language are words that can still express dissent. The gaps in feeling are the discomfort contradiction produces. The gaps in fact are things that can still be brought out and checked against an account.
They intend to close every one of those gaps.
Once that is done, there will be nowhere left in a person's mind from which a question can arise. It is not that he dare not ask. There is nothing left to ask about.
What this machinery wants is not control. It is completion.
And can it be done?
We can now put the question that really drives this series.
This is an attempt at closure.
Not oppression, not rule, not exploitation: those are ordinary enough; history is full of them. This machinery seeks to cover a person completely, leaving no gap at all.
And the novel spends four hundred pages on one question:
Can it be done?
The main narrative appears to answer yes. In the end, Winston loves Big Brother. He has been remade completely. He is not merely giving in; he means it. He believes it himself.
This is the most complete defeat in the history of literature.
But the book contains something else, after the main narrative ends.
At the back is an appendix called “The Principles of Newspeak.”
The great majority of readers skip it, because it reads like a linguistic explanation: the grammar of Newspeak, the three categories of vocabulary, the technical details.
And that appendix has a feature almost no one notices.
It is written in the past tense.
The next essay will not discuss that yet. It will discuss Winston and Julia: the little room they rent, the glass paperweight, what they think they have managed to keep.
Because before they were arrested, they really did keep something.
And what that something was deserves a clear look.
George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949. Names and terms in the Chinese essay follow Dong Leshan's translation.

review.full_reread: Read all four Chinese bodies and all four complete en translations, titles, decks and index. Reread every changed unit against the final approved wording and its surrounding argument. Earlier review evidence is retained in review_history, not current pending status.
review.structure: All paragraph, heading and inline-emphasis boundaries preserved; all unamended prose units unchanged.
review.interpretive_boundaries: Original authorial judgments retained. Source observations outside the approved change set remain historical context; this pass makes no new claim of exhaustive independent novel or publication-history verification.
semantic_checks: Photograph: conscious recognition and concealment, then destruction after about ten minutes through fear; no reflex or pre-awareness claim remains.
Private life: the Brotherhood attempt remains explicit, while value exceeds usefulness to resistance; deliberate suppression of sexual pleasure is not confused with a forgotten prohibition.
Dress is a future intention while Julia remains in overalls; lipstick replaces the invented worn dress in both sensory examples.
Julia rejects the earlier dead claim and repeats it only just before arrest; present life is distinguished from distant political victory.
Cross-references now point to essay three; forbidden book arrives later through a briefcase exchange.
Pain is controlled by a dial, without asserting an electrical mechanism; the two final sentences are the ending of the main narrative.
Publication: American Book-of-the-Month Club deletion request and refusal; the importance of final placement is explicitly the essay’s reading.

Proles: less intensive ideological training coexists with surveillance and removal of threats; no blanket illiteracy claim; the courtyard is reached by power without exhausting the meaning of the song.

Preserved the complete room/trap/real-experience argument, authorial claim that past events cannot be undone, stronger judgment about totality, and cautious appendix reading without supplying a new proof or ending.

review.coverage: All 86 source units translated in order, including six headings, the series question, the appendix foreshadowing, and the source note.
prior_edition_findings: The previous approximately 495-word rewriting omitted the three-part machinery as a sustained sequence, the photograph, Syme's disappearance, the definitive-edition argument, and the open question linking the four essays.
Its added discussion of modern euphemism and linguistic determinism replaced the author's sequence and has not been carried forward.

source_questions.issue: The Chinese calls destruction of the photograph an unconscious reflex. Part I, Chapter 7 describes recognition, concealment, and roughly ten minutes of fearful waiting. Retained pending author decision.
Syme's intelligence as the reason for his disappearance is Winston's interpretation, not a separately confirmed official explanation. Author's reading retained.
The forward reference says essay four; the detailed dismantling of arithmetic and inward refusal is in essay three, with synthesis in essay four. Retained pending editorial decision.

review.style: Short paragraphs, repetitions, emphasis, and unanswered question preserved; no new theoretical resolution added.
